transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-15 14:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Ava Monroe (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Reef Health - Head of ML), Tom Hargreaves (CTO), Lila Nguyen (Platform Engineer)

Auto-summary (auto gen):
- Reef Health is evaluating a move off a mixed stack (OpenAI + Anthropic + on-prem vLLM) toward a single inference platform; main concerns: eval parity, latency at 99th, cost, and data residency/SOC2.
- Redwood options discussed: Hosted for quick PoC, Dedicated reserved capacity for predictable SLA, Private/VPC for sensitive PHI flows.

Topics:
- Current stack details (OpenAI/Anthropic usage, TGI/vLLM on prem)
- Parity testing approach (metrics, seed, prompt sets)
- Networking and security (VPC peering, KMS, SAML SSO, audit logs)
- Performance expectations and bottlenecks (KV cache, batching, latency SLOs)
- Commercial ask: pricing expectations for Dedicated pilot

Transcript body:
[00:00] Ava Monroe: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, quick intros?
[00:12] Maya Patel: hi all, i'm maya, i run the ml team at reef health, we do automated medical summarization and clinical triage, um we're evaluating our inference stack.
[00:25] Tom Hargreaves: tom here, cto, probably mostly listening but will jump on infra questions.
[00:31] Lila Nguyen: lila, platform eng, i manage k8s and the vpc stuff.
[00:36] Diego Ramos: diego from redwood, i'm the se on the account, i'll dive into perf and the porting details.
[00:43] Ava Monroe: thanks. So quick context — i saw your note, you're running a hybrid approach, openai for high-quality chat, anthropic for safety-like checks, plus some on-prem vLLM for PII-sensitive payloads, is that right?
[01:00] Maya Patel: yeah that's correct. we picked openai for the chat models, anthropic for a safety layer on some pipelines, and we also have tgi/vllm locally for cost-sensitive batch inference.
[01:13] Tom Hargreaves: plus we have a mandate from legal to keep PHI on-prem unless encrypted and audited — so private deployment is a likely requirement for parts of the workload.
[01:24] Ava Monroe: super helpful, thanks. can you walk me through your main success criteria for a migration or consolidation? what must be identical or better?
[01:34] Maya Patel: ogll, the top-line is eval parity — we have a bunch of human-rated prompts and automated metrics (EM, F1, hallucination rate). if outputs change significantly, product will flag it. we also care about 99th percentile latency under 2s for chat flows and cost per 1k tokens not exceeding our current spend by more than 10%.
[01:55] Diego Ramos: quick clarifying q — when you say 2s 99th, that's for streaming token latency or for full response completion?
[02:03] Maya Patel: full response completion for interactive clinical triage, average response maybe 800 tokens.
[02:10] Lila Nguyen: additionally we need to know about certs and KMS integration, we can't have key material leave our VPC.
[02:17] Ava Monroe: understood. so there are three levers: model variants (we can run exact same open weights if available), quantization/profiles, and runtime configs like batching and kv caching. for parity we generally recommend a staged approach — host a parity eval with our hosted catalog first, then a dedicated pilot and finally private if you need on-prem.
[02:38] Tom Hargreaves: what's the delta typically when you port from a managed openai flavor to a local vLLM run? we saw some drift with TGI before.
[02:48] Diego Ramos: good q — drift can be from tokenization differences, sampling seeds, or different fused kernels. we usually control for tokenizer and sampling (same vocab, same seed) and run the same prompt set. performance-wise vLLM/TGI can be faster for batch, but for small streaming chat the optimized kernels in our runtime + kv cache often beat generic vLLM unless you have heavy sequence reuse.
[03:09] Maya Patel: and how do you handle the Anthropic safety checks — can we chain models? our current pipeline sends responses to anthropic for a second pass.
[03:19] Ava Monroe: yes, you can chain or run parallel calls; Redwood supports routing and fallback rules so you can keep a safety model in the loop. for Hosted we have preconfigured endpoints, for Dedicated you can pin model versions and create routing policies that send copies to the safety cluster.
[03:35] Lila Nguyen: re networking, if we wanted Private: what's the control plane model, does any traffic go through redwood infra?
[03:42] Diego Ramos: with Private (VPC) the control plane is customer-controlled, and data-plane can be fully in your VPC if you opt for on-prem package. short-lived metadata may touch the control plane for orchestration but payloads can be kept in your network and keys in your KMS/HSM. we can provide architecture diagrams.
[03:59] Tom Hargreaves: SOC2 and audit retention — do you preserve request/response logs by default? we need 13 months retention for audits.
[04:07] Ava Monroe: Hosted keeps token metadata, but for PHI use cases we recommend Dedicated/Private with configurable retention. we can hand over logs to S3 in your account or integrate with your SIEM. we'll send the SOC2 pack.
[04:22] Maya Patel: great. also, when you run parity evals, do you support exact seeding for stochastic sampling? our eval harness uses nucleus sampling with top-p 0.9 and temperature 0.2.
[04:33] Diego Ramos: yes, we'll reproduce sampling parameters and set deterministic seeds where supported. a caveat: some kernels or quantized models may not support perfect bitwise parity; we aim for metric parity within your tolerance.
[04:46] Ava Monroe: can we talk about costs — both per-token hosted and the economics of Dedicated reserved capacity?
[04:53] Tom Hargreaves: we're particularly concerned about burst traffic during support hours, so unpredictable spikes are expensive.
[04:59] Diego Ramos: Hosted is good for experimentation; Dedicated lets you reserve GPUs and smooth cost per token. we also have autoscale and burst capacity options so you can meet spikes without massive over-provisioning. we'll provide ballpark numbers in the follow-up.
[05:12] Maya Patel: technical deep dive question — kv cache behavior, we rely on long context reuse across sessions; how do you handle migrating that workload so we don't lose cache benefits?
[05:23] Diego Ramos: the runtime preserves prefix KV cache and supports shared cache policies. when migrating, we can warm caches using your logs or replay traces; we also support hot shards for high-reuse keys.
[05:34] Lila Nguyen: ok, about the PII workloads — if we do Private, can we bring our own HSM and KMS?
[05:40] Ava Monroe: yes, BYO-KMS/HSM is supported for Private. we'll map the key references and provide key wrapping guidance.
[05:47] Speaker 5: [inaudible]...
[05:50] Diego Ramos: small note on toolchain — our CI/CD integrates with model rollouts, canary / gradual traffic, and automatic rollback if quality regresses. we tie regressions to eval sets so you get alerts.
[06:06] Maya Patel: that's useful. we have a defined QA prompt set for regression checks. we need to understand the false positive rate when you run canary checks.
[06:17] Diego Ramos: we can tune thresholds; you set the trigger for rollback. we'll propose defaults but you'll own the thresholds.
[06:24] Ava Monroe: maybe a quick demo would help after you share prompt sets, but i'm mindful of not doing a full-run in this call.
[06:31] Tom Hargreaves: timeline question — if we started a pilot now, how long to get a meaningful parity readout?
[06:36] Diego Ramos: typically 2 weeks for a baseline parity run on hosted, 3–4 weeks for Dedicated pilot including infra setup and more exhaustive load tests. Private on-prem adds provisioning time (depends on your windows).
[06:49] Maya Patel: ok that's reasonable. can you outline what you need from us to kick off the hosted parity run?
[06:55] Ava Monroe: yes — sample prompt set, evaluation harness or scripts, a list of models and exact params you're using on OpenAI/Anthropic, and a small dataset for performance warmup. we'll send a benchmark template.
[07:08] Lila Nguyen: firewalls — we have a strict egress policy, so we'll need specific IPs for hosted or use a proxy.
[07:15] Diego Ramos: we can support static egress IPs and provide documentation; Dedicated and Private avoid egress issues since they stay in your VPC.
[07:24] Maya Patel: one more question on model compatibility — we use a few fine-tuned checkpoints internally on tgi; will you support importing those weights or replicating the fine-tune in your runtime?
[07:35] Diego Ramos: we can import standard formats (pt, safetensors) and run them in the Dedicated/Private runtimes. we'll check compatibility for any custom operators. for Hosted, we offer a limited import path depending on governance.
[07:46] Ava Monroe: noted. regarding benchmarks, do you have a target throughput?
[07:50] Tom Hargreaves: for batch nightly reports we do 30k tokens/minute, but interactive is small qps with tight tail limits.
[07:58] Diego Ramos: sounds like a mixed workload — we'll design the pilot to test both modes.
[08:04] Maya Patel: what about quantization? we rely on FP16 in prod but would consider int8 for cost savings if accuracy holds.
[08:11] Diego Ramos: we'll run quantization experiments and include quant profiles in the report. we typically recommend int8 only after verifying metric drift.
[08:20] Ava Monroe: quick note on procurement — do you have procurement constraints like PO terms, or is this a card-based start?
[08:27] Tom Hargreaves: for POC likely card, but enterprise purchase will need contract and PO.
[08:31] Ava Monroe: ok we'll prepare both pathways.
[08:34] Maya Patel: anything else on the risk side? model divergence is our biggest. if outputs drift, product will push back.
[08:41] Diego Ramos: to mitigate we'll run side-by-side comparisons and provide delta reports per prompt and aggregate metrics; also we can enable a dual-run period where both systems run in parallel and we slowly route traffic.
[08:55] Lila Nguyen: what's the instrumentation like for tracing requests to model versions? we need distributed traces.
[09:00] Diego Ramos: we emit traces and per-token latency breakdowns; you can hook up to existing tracing backends.
[09:06] Ava Monroe: ok i want to recap the next steps and owners...
[09:10] Ava Monroe: diego will draft the benchmark plan and sample harness, maya will share prompts and metrics, lila will share infra constraints, and i will send pricing and security docs.
[09:20] Tom Hargreaves: sounds good.
[09:22] Maya Patel: thanks, we'll review and sync on the scoping call next week.

End of transcript.
